title: Imperial War Council (Hofkriegsrat), Vienna, to Johann Ludwig von Kuefstein, imperial orator, 27 Oct 1629 (catalogue 2236): read with Donath's printed alphabet of Kuefstein's cipher, tested on her three glossed specimens

steps.what: Donath 1964 article PDF fetched once from EPA; the plate (p. 57) and the key and specimen pages (pp. 58-62) extracted at full scan size.
Catalogue vetting record, Donath 1964, Lang 2015 entry, one web search, Szabados 2024 text: no decipherment of p. 1461 found.
Sign conventions written first; two passes from different crops, reconciled on close-ups.
Donath's p. 58 alphabet mapped to the plate's shapes and frozen (key_frozen.tsv) with two nulls fixed from the plate.
Held-out: Donath's three glossed specimens (pp. 615, 1069, 755), 373 of 377 signs (98.9%) give her gloss with the frozen key. Not independent of Donath's own key work.

Mechanical decryption read as German; check_marks.py passes (no changed or added letters). 99 of 102 cipher words taken verbatim, 3 holes (opening code group and a two-sign group). Reading checker: 0.50 in the writer's spelling (period spellings unknown to the word list), 0.90 normalised.

Blind review by a separate AI language-model agent: four plate lines copied sign by sign before opening the transcription (4/4 agree), decryption, mark check and held-out test re-run, reading read as sentences. It agreed with the state read (grade B) and asked for four fixes.

Fixes from the review: L06 'dan' (signs q oo o-) marked doubtful as [?man], since the first sign may be d (m) not q (d) on the halftone; translation follows; sign conventions brought into line with the tokens used; the reading-file checker figure corrected. Now 98 of 102 words verbatim, 1 guess, 3 holes; check_marks.py passes.

Integration check (12 Nov 2026) by a reader who took no part: sha256 of key_frozen.tsv matches FROZEN.sha256; heldout.py re-run 373/377 = 98.9%; check_marks.py 18 lines, 0 unmarked; a separate decoder written from key_frozen.tsv reproduces decryption_p1461.txt line by line; the EPA PDF fetched again and the plate (p. 57) and printed table (p. 58) looked at (opening words and the clear date and subscription agree; no sign-by-sign recheck at high zoom). 98 of 102 = 96.1% recounted. Catalogue 2236 corrected (Hofkriegsrat to Kuefstein). No change to the texts.

outcome.method_basis: Alphabet printed by Donath 1964 p. 58 for Kuefstein's cipher (rebuilt by her from glossed drafts in the same volume), mapped to the plate's sign shapes, frozen, tested on her three glossed specimens, and applied to the bare page p. 1461. The key is partial only in that the opening code group is not decrypted.
outcome.fraction_read_source: reading_p1461.md: 98 of 102 cipher words read verbatim from the signs (1 guess, 3 holes).

texts.label: p. 1461, Hofkriegsrat to Kuefstein, Vienna, 27 Oct 1629
texts.summary: The sender (probably the Emperor, the subject being the open opening group) has learned from Kuefstein's letter how he was received at Ofen (Buda) by some 3,000 Turks; the War Council asks, apparently on the Emperor's order (the subject is the open opening group), Kuefstein to report what troops these were, whether they came from Ofen or from other Turkish places and borders, and whether they have dispersed or are still together.
texts.note: 98 of 102 cipher words verbatim from the signs, 1 guess ([?man] in L06, where the signs give 'dan'), 3 holes (the opening code group [1] [2], most likely a code for the Emperor, and the two-sign group [3] before 'herrn'). The holes and the guess are all in the first sentence.

reading_review.note: Reads as continuous Hofkriegsrat chancery prose; about 98 of 102 words make sense from the signs, and four plate lines checked sign by sign agree with the transcription. Grade B because the opening code group is unread, 'dan' in L06 is doubtful (now marked [?man]), the only image is a 1964 halftone, and the held-out test does not cover the values fixed on the plate.

gaps.item: Opening code group [1] [2] (L01) and the two-sign group [3] before 'herrn' (L03)
gaps.detail: Do not decrypt with the letter key; [1] [2] most likely stands for the Emperor. A code list for this cipher would settle them.
The first sign may be d (m) rather than q (d); the 1964 halftone does not settle it.
Only the Donath 1964 halftone plate was seen; the clear heading and subscription, and the doubtful signs, need ELTE's original or a better image.

prior.where: Donath 1964 p. 58 prints the letter alphabet and deciphers three other letters of the volume (Tom. V pp. 615, 755, 1069); no decipherment of p. 1461 printed. Lang 2015 marks it undeciphered. Checked 12 Nov 2026: one web search, Szabados 2024 (Acta Historica 148) text searched; catalogue vetting of 4 Nov 2026 (DECODE, Tomokiyo, Lasry).

human: WAINUT set the task (catalogue 2236) and the rules; AI language-model agents transcribed, mapped and froze the key, ran the held-out test, read and checked, and a separate AI language-model agent reviewed the result blind. No target-specific human intervention. No human palaeographer checked the text.
